subject: science
topic: Species are vanishing far faster than the natural rate
angle: While official records of extinction are low, data on vertebrate species and genera suggest current loss rates are significantly higher than background levels.
title: The speed of extinction

hooks.text: What happens when a species disappears forever?
The records are low, but the loss is high.
You are living in a period of rapid loss.
A land snail in the dirt.

reveal.headline: We may have already lost 7% of the species on Earth.
reveal.body: Extrapolation from a random sample of land snail species suggests 130,000 extinctions have already occurred.

explain.headline: Vertebrate loss is exceeding natural rates.
explain.body: The average rate of vertebrate species loss over the last century is up to 100 times higher than the background rate.

matters.headline: The crisis is hidden in the numbers.
matters.body: Official records of extinction are low. That may be why the scale of the loss feels smaller than the data suggests.

example.headline: The woods behind your house.
example.body: You walk past the same trees every day. You do not see the species that are no longer there to occupy the space.

question.headline: What will be gone by your time?

claims.text: Only 799 (0.04%) of the 1.9 million known recent species are recorded as extinct, which questions the reality of the crisis.
claims.quote: only 799 (0.04%) of the 1.9 million known recent species are recorded as extinct, questioning the reality of the crisis.

claims.text: Extrapolation from a random sample of land snail species suggests we may already have lost 7% (130,000 extinctions) of the species on Earth.
claims.quote: we may already have lost 7% (130,000 extinctions) of the species on Earth.

claims.text: In a sample of nearly half of known vertebrate species, 32% (8,851/27,600) are decreasing in population size and range.
claims.quote: In our sample, comprising nearly half of known vertebrate species, 32% (8,851/27,600) are decreasing; that is, they have decreased in population size and range.

claims.text: In 177 mammals with detailed data, all have lost 30% or more of their geographic ranges and more than 40% of the species have experienced severe population declines.
claims.quote: In the 177 mammals for which we have detailed data, all have lost 30% or more of their geographic ranges and more than 40% of the species have experienced severe population declines (>80% range shrinkage).

claims.text: If all now-endangered genera were to vanish by 2,100, extinction rates would be 354 (average) or 511 (for mammals) times higher than background rates.

verdict: The evidence indicates that vertebrate species and genera are being lost at rates far exceeding natural background levels, though the total number of known extinctions remains low.
caveat: Many estimates of the extinction crisis are based on extrapolations or focus on vertebrates, potentially masking the status of invertebrates which represent the bulk of biodiversity.
caption:
Species are vanishing faster than the natural rate.

Data on vertebrate species and genera show loss rates far exceeding background levels, though many estimates rely on extrapolations. These figures may mask the status of invertebrates, which make up the bulk of biodiversity.
